newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Weather delays spring sowing in Yugoslavia.
newsitem.headline: Weather delays spring sowing in Yugoslavia.

text.p: Bad weather and a lack of funds have delayed Yugoslavia's spring sowing campaign, which has been completed on some 650,000 hectares out of 2.3 million ha planned, analysts said on Tuesday.
"Spring sowing is delayed on some 100,000 ha compared to last year," Milan Prostran, assistant to the federal agriculture minister, told Reuters.
Unfavourable weather and the government's inability to pay outstanding debts to farmers for the 1996 crop had affected this year's spring campaign.

"The targeted area under industrial crops will certainly be well below estimated acreage, primarily due to economic reasons and bad weather," said Ljiljana Vasic, head of the association of agricultural cooperatives in the country's bread-basket of Vojvodina.
Maize area was expected to rise by at least 100,000 ha at the expense of sugar beet and sunflower, Prostran added.
Maize area for 1997 was set at 1.4 million ha, with the campaign in full swing now, analysts added.

"We expect the maize area of 650,000 ha targeted for Vojvodina plus an additional 75,000-100,000 ha to be sown by May 10. The soil has been prepared much better than the previous year and temperatures are good," Lazo Jakovljevic of the Farming Institute of Novi Sad said.
Farmers failed to meet a targeted 100,000 ha sugar beet area and planted only some 60,000 ha, again mainly because of delayed debt payments by the government and bad weather.
"Low temperatures have seriously effected large beet areas, especially the early planted crop," said Lazo Kovacev, another Novi Sad analyst.
The sugar beet campaign started at the beginning of March because of favourable weather, but frosts in the week that began on April 9 hit the newly emerging crop.
"Some 20,000 ha under beet has already been re-sown and the crop on another 10,000 ha is under threat," Kovacev said.
Farmers have been urged to complete re-planting by the end of the week.
The target for sunflower was 200,000 ha, but analysts doubted whether that would be met, with only 80,000 ha planted so far.
Vasic said it was unlikely farmers would sow the rest of the planned sunflower area before the end of the campaign on May 15.
"Sugar and oil refineries have still not paid farmers for their 1996 crops."
Some 16,000 ha had been planted to soy out of 80,000 ha planned and 90,000 ha out of 190,000 had been planted to fodder crops.
"Only sowing of grain is above the target," Prostran said. Food grains were planted on some 118,400 ha, slightly above 108,200 ha planned.
He said the government had secured enough seed, herbicide and fuel for the crops. There would even be enough fertiliser as domestic production was expected to reach 500,000 tonnes.
That was less than half the quantity used in 1990 but more than the 300,000 tonnes consumed last year, he added.
